source.title: Neural Networks with Finite Intrinsic Dimension have no Spurious Valleys
source.authors: Luca Venturi; A. Bandeira; Joan Bruna

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, titled “Spurious Valleys in One-hidden-layer Neural Network Optimization Landscapes”; the title in the ID metadata differs. No relevant sections appear cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical results about spurious valleys in one-hidden-layer networks, a landscape property related to but distinct from gradient training reaching low training classification error. It tests aspects of V2 through width-dependent results for quadratic networks, but does not test V2’s ReLU teacher-student setting or its stated gradient-descent frequency claim. Its other results do not directly test the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports mathematical results and constructions, not benchmark classification-error measurements or gradient-training runs. Relevant result rows record the paper’s explicit statements about absence or presence of spurious valleys and its width conditions. Cited results from other papers are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study proves loss-landscape properties and existence of non-increasing paths, rather than testing any listed version. In particular, V2 concerns gradient-descent failure frequencies in realizable ReLU teacher-student problems and the effect of one or two extra student neurons. Neither the general landscape theorems nor the worst-case constructions establish those outcomes. Section 6 explicitly says the positive landscape results do not guarantee gradient-descent convergence.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. Finite intrinsic dimension supplies sufficient width conditions for absence of spurious valleys, while adverse distributions can produce arbitrarily bad valleys at any width for the stated nonnegative nonpolynomial activations. The generic-setting conclusion should be stated probabilistically: under the stated assumptions, random initialization admits non-increasing paths to increasingly low risk with high probability as width increases. This does not assert that every valley has low risk or guarantee gradient-descent performance.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies loss-landscape topology for one-hidden-layer networks using theoretical arguments; it does not run the benchmark gradient-training recipes in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The theoretical conclusions depend on activation class, data distribution, width relative to intrinsic dimension or sample count, loss assumptions, and in Theorem 16 initialization and regularity conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Sufficient width relative to intrinsic dimension or sample count guarantees absence of spurious valleys; improved guarantees cover arbitrary-width linear networks and scalar-output quadratic networks with p ≥ 2n + 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sufficient overparameterization can remove spurious valleys in specified neural-network loss landscapes.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructed distributions yield arbitrarily bad spurious valleys below a lower-intrinsic-dimension bound, and at every finite width for the stated nonnegative nonpolynomial activations, including ReLU.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width alone cannot eliminate worst-case spurious valleys for nonnegative nonpolynomial activations without assumptions on the data distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: With random first-layer initialization and the stated assumptions, increasing width gives high-probability existence of non-increasing paths to population risk approaching the irreducible-risk baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing width improves probabilistic low-risk path guarantees, without establishing gradient-descent convergence.

record.problems: The findings are theoretical landscape statements rather than measurements of training classification error or optimization trajectories. Negative results use constructed worst-case distributions; the authors state that absence of high-energy barriers is insufficient to guarantee convergence of local descent algorithms and that their work is not informative about gradient-descent performance in regimes without spurious valleys.

untested.parts: All parts: convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, label corruption, model size, stopping, and regularization.

All parts: realizable ReLU teacher-student problems, gradient descent from standard initialization, failure frequencies as both widths grow, and the effect of one or two extra student neurons at widths 6–20.
All parts: depth-related training degradation, identity shortcuts, batch-normalized convolutional networks, special tanh initialization, and Fixup.
All parts: activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, learning speed, trainable depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
All parts: learning-rate stability thresholds, transient loss increases, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence.
All parts: batch normalization's effect on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparable training without normalization using Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are assessed against the supplied claim versions; cannot_determine does not dispute the theorem statements. The paper's discussion of Safran and Shamir is cited evidence, not a new test of V2. No verdict labels apply.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, model size, stopping, and regularization recipes.

The paper discusses landscape properties and width, but does not test the ReLU teacher-student problem, gradient descent from standard initialization, or how often optimization ends in spurious minima as teacher and student widths grow.
Plain versus residual networks, depth, batch normalization, ImageNet/CIFAR-10 training error, Fixup, and very deep plain tanh networks.
Initialization comparisons, training speed, trainable depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NNs Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 8 proves absence of spurious valleys when the width meets the finite upper intrinsic dimension.

conditions.value: continuous σ and X with finite upper intrinsic dimension

rows.measure: presence or absence of spurious valleys
rows.value: no spurious valleys in the over-parametrised regime p ≥ dim*(σ, X)
rows.note: This is a theoretical landscape result, not an observed gradient-descent outcome or V2 teacher-student frequency measurement.
rows.check: Theorem 8 establishes absence of spurious valleys under an intrinsic-dimension width bound; it does not establish V2's gradient-descent outcomes or teacher-student width comparison.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NNs Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Corollary 9 gives absence of spurious valleys for empirical risk on N data points.

conditions.value: empirical loss with convex per-example loss

rows.measure: presence or absence of spurious valleys
rows.value: no spurious valleys in the over-parametrized regime p ≥ N
rows.note: The result is stated as a theorem; the paper notes it was already shown in Livni et al. (2014).
rows.check: The empirical-risk landscape guarantee at p ≥ N does not measure gradient-descent failure frequencies or adding one or two neurons beyond a teacher. The authors acknowledge a prior result but also present their own corollary allowing rank degeneracy.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NNs Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.size_stated: width p ≥ the stated polynomial-dimension bound
rows.operation_detail: Corollary 10 gives absence of spurious valleys for polynomial activations under a width bound.

conditions.value: σ(z) = a0 + a1 z + ··· + ad z^d

rows.measure: presence or absence of spurious valleys
rows.value: no spurious valleys for p ≥ Σ from i=1 to d of binomial(n+i−1, i) 1{ai ≠ 0}
rows.note: A theoretical sufficient width condition; not an empirical width sweep.
rows.check: This is a sufficient width bound for polynomial-activation landscapes, outside V2's ReLU teacher-student setting and optimization-outcome measure.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer linear NNs Φ(x; θ) = UWx
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 11 proves absence of spurious valleys for linear networks of any depth and widths.
rows.measure: presence or absence of spurious valleys
rows.note: The theorem states no over-parametrisation is required.
rows.check: The subject should be linear networks of arbitrary depth, Φ(x; θ) = W_(K+1)…W_1 x, rather than only one-hidden-layer networks. Absence of spurious valleys in these networks tests none of the listed versions.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NNs Φ(x; θ) = uTσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 12 proves absence of spurious valleys for quadratic networks with scalar output.
rows.measure: presence or absence of spurious valleys
rows.note: The paper says the factor 2 is due to proof technicalities and that extending to p ≥ n is left as a possibility.
rows.check: Quadratic-network landscape guarantees at p ≥ 2n + 1 do not test V2's ReLU teacher-student gradient-descent claim.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NNs Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 13 constructs a data distribution yielding spurious valleys when width is no more than half the lower intrinsic dimension.

conditions.value: non-negative σ in the stated square-integrability class

rows.measure: presence of spurious valleys and loss gap
rows.value: spurious valleys exist; for any M > 0, a distribution can be chosen with a non-empty open set whose loss is at least M above the minimum and whose escape path must climb at least M
rows.note: This is a worst-case theoretical construction. It does not test the frequency of gradient-descent convergence failures in V2.
rows.check: This worst-case distribution construction does not establish realizability, standard-initialization failure frequencies, or V2's teacher-relative width effect. Correct the barrier statement: the text guarantees an uphill increase of at least M/2 from the starting point, with the path maximum at least M above the minimum over Ω; the suboptimality gap is at least M.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NNs Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Corollary 15 states existence of arbitrarily bad spurious valleys for non-polynomial activations under a constructed data distribution.

conditions.value: continuous, non-negative, non-polynomial σ in the stated square-integrability class

rows.measure: presence of spurious valleys and loss gap
rows.value: arbitrarily bad spurious valleys exist for any hidden layer width p ≥ 1
rows.note: The result is existential and worst-case, not a gradient-training trial.
rows.check: Existence of an adverse distribution for every width, including ReLU networks, does not test V2's specified realizable teacher-student setting or failure-frequency comparison.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NNs Φ(x; θ) = uTσ(Wx)
rows.size_stated: width p with stated lower bounds
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 16 constructs non-increasing paths from sampled initial first-layer weights to low-loss solutions with high probability.

conditions.value: w̃i sampled i.i.d. uniformly over the unit sphere

rows.measure: endpoint loss along a non-increasing path
rows.value: L(θ1) ≤ R(X, Y) + λ if p ≥ O(−λ−1 log(λδ)), with probability at least 1−δ; under the stated regularity, L(θ1) ≤ R(X, Y) + O(p^(−1+δ)) with probability at least 1−e^(−O(p^δ))
rows.note: This establishes theoretical paths and endpoint loss bounds, not gradient-descent training-error outcomes.
rows.check: Existence of a non-increasing path to low population risk does not establish gradient-descent behavior or initialization-dependent training speed. Include Remark 17's bias convention: augmented weight-and-bias vectors are sampled on S^n.
